findings.evidence: 36-word sentence, 4 subordinate-clause markers: Then, the review takes longer because the manager who normally handles it is traveling; the backup reviewer who covers for absences was not told that the request needs sign-off before the portal releases the confirmation email.
findings.violation: The sentence runs to 36 words with 4 subordinate-clause markers, longer than the reader can hold in mind on a single pass.
findings.fix: Split the sentence at a subordinate-clause boundary.

findings.evidence: If the position counts as full-time, the stipend can apply. If the employee has completed 90 days of continuous service, the stipend can apply. If the request arrives before the benefit year ends, the stipend can apply. Only once every condition above is met does the home-office equipment stipend become available to the employee.
findings.violation: Three separate sentences each state a single condition as though it alone makes the stipend apply, and only the fourth sentence reveals the actual governing rule, that all three conditions must be met together. A reader who stops after the first sentence, or reads them as independent triggers rather than a joint requirement, forms a wrong belief about eligibility.
findings.fix: Open the paragraph with the governing rule, for example the stipend requires all of the following, then list the three conditions under it.

findings.evidence: Consecutive sentence subjects across the paragraph's four sentences: the position, the employee, the request, every condition above.
findings.violation: Each of the paragraph's four sentences opens with a new grammatical subject unconnected to the subject the sentence before it established, so the reader has to re-orient at every sentence boundary instead of tracking one running topic.
findings.fix: Restate the paragraph around one running subject, for example the employee or the stipend, across all four sentences, or combine the three conditions into a single sentence under one subject.

findings.evidence: Program Overview: The people operations office publishes the reimbursement log each quarter. Overview: The benefits team publishes the reimbursement log after every open enrollment period.
findings.violation: Two sections name a different owner for the reimbursement log, the people operations office in Program Overview versus the benefits team in Overview, and a different publication cadence, each quarter versus after every open enrollment period, with no signal whether the two sections describe the same process or two different ones.
findings.fix: State the reimbursement log's owner and publication cadence once, in one section, and remove or reconcile the duplicate Overview section.

findings.violation: The heading text matches the fixed list of non-specific heading labels, so a reader scanning headings cannot tell whether the section applies to them.
findings.fix: Replace the heading with text specific enough to be found by scanning.

findings.evidence: The finance office reviews every stipend request over 200 dollars before it pays out. The finance office also flags any request that repeats within the same quarter.
findings.violation: The section describes an internal finance-office review threshold and audit flag, content written for an internal reviewer rather than the employee applying for the stipend, with no signal marking it as background rather than an instruction the reader must follow.
findings.fix: Move the internal review criteria to an internal reference, or add a sentence stating that this section describes finance's own process and requires no action from the employee.

findings.evidence: The manager approves items pursuant to internal discretion, notwithstanding the standard review checklist.
findings.violation: The sentence uses a legal or foreign-language jargon term from the fixed list with no plain-language definition in the same or the following sentence.
findings.fix: Replace the jargon term with a plain equivalent, or define it at first use.

findings.evidence: Request Steps is the 9th of the document's 13 sections, appearing after Approval Timeline, Required Documentation, Reimbursement Amounts, Restrictions and Exceptions, and Terminology Notes.
findings.violation: The section stating the actual step sequence for completing a request, confirming eligibility then uploading the receipt, appears well after sections the reader only needs once a request is already underway, instead of sitting with or immediately after How to Apply, where the reader needs it to start.
findings.fix: Move Request Steps next to How to Apply, or merge its content into that section.
